Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

School & learning

university noun

also universities, go to university, uni, college

modern

Traupman 400
M-O s.v. school types: university, after Egger
Levi–Bini p. 67

ūniversitās studiōrum, ūniversitātis studiōrum f.

a university

Classically ūniversitās is the whole, and in the jurists a corporation (Gai. Inst. 2.11, Lewis & Short); the guilds of masters and students that became the universities took the name in the Middle Ages. Studiōrum makes the sense plain; Traupman also allows ūniversitās alone.

Other words

  • 1acadēmīa: long i (Traupman 28 and Morgan–Owens acadēmia). Cicero’s own verse scans it long: Inque Acadēmīā umbriferā nitidōque Lycēō (Div. 1.22), where -dēmī- makes a spondee before the elided final -ā. Lewis & Short: long in Cicero and in Tullius Laurea (ap. Plin. NH 31.8), short only in Claudian and Sidonius. Greek Ἀκαδήμεια.

    acadēmīa1, acadēmīae f. — a university

    noun, first declension · also used · Renaissance · M-O s.v. school types: university, after Vives (1540), Mercator (1595) and Tursellinus (1652); Traupman 28, 267 (academy)

    The humanists’ word for a university. Classically the gymnasium outside Athens where Plato taught, and the name Cicero gave to his villa near Puteoli and to a gymnasium at his Tusculan villa (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • in Valentīnā Acadēmīā (ūniversitātem vocant) tōtō orbe celeberrimā

    at the Academy of Valencia (they call it a university), the most famous in the whole worldRuiz (1794), p. viii, quoted by Morgan–Owens s.v. school types: university

See also college, student, education, school.
